newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Chances of EMU up as core group closes in. [CORRECTED 14:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Chances of EMU up as core group closes in. [CORRECTED 14:51 GMT]

text.p: (Replaces and corrects previous story. Clarifies presentation of results following adjustments to some questions in this month's questionnaire.)
By Pratima Desai
Chances of European currency union starting on time seem to be improving because fewer countries are expected to qualify from the outset, EMU analysts said in a Reuters survey published on Thursday.

Forty three analysts were asked to predict the likelihood of European economic and monetary union (EMU) going ahead on the planned launch date of January 1, 1999. The average response gave EMU an 80 percent chance of starting on time, up from 76 percent in March. In February, the average prediction was 83 percent.

This month's poll adjusted some subsidiary questions about potential EMU members to gauge more finely the perceived likelihood of individual countries' participation. Respondents were asked to give a percentage likelihood of each country joining at the start (explains adjustments to this month's poll).

Of the forecasts which gave a country-by-country breakdown, only Germany, France and the Netherlands were unanimously forecast as being founder members of currency union. These countries were rated 100 percent likely to join at the start by 100 percent of respondents...(clarifies percentages).
One contributor had doubts about Luxembourg's certain entry into the first wave, six expressed reservations over Belgium and seven wondered about Austria's membership from the start.

The forecasters having doubts about Austria and Belgium said the two countries were having difficulty in meeting two of the entry requirements for EMU -- a target budget deficit at three percent of gross domestic product(GDP) or less and total debt at 60 percent of GDP or less.
Because of its currency union with Belgium, Luxembourg may be left out by default, according to one contributor.
Germany is not expected to meet the entry targets set out in the Maastricht treaty, but some method will be found to bend the rules as EMU without Germany is not feasible, the analysts said.

"As it stands the treaty allows for exceptional circumstances to be taken into account. Germany can claim they are still suffering from re-unification," said Terry Baker, economist at the Economic and Social Research Institute of Ireland.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision two weeks ago to stand for re-election in the German elections in 1998 was cited as a major reason for the upward revision in the Reuters EMU barometer.
"He is standing again with the express purpose of making sure EMU starts on time and the transition is smooth," said Klaus Baader, currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

The number of experts believing Ireland and Finland were certain to be in EMU at the start dropped since March. Seventeen out of 38, or 45 percent, of respondents in April gave each country a 100 percent chance of founder membership. In March 37 out of 45 people, or 82 percent, ticked Finland as a first wave entrant and 38 out of 45 -- 84 percent -- did the same for Ireland...(clarifies presentation of results as number of responses for each country).

The survey showed the perceived chances for Britain, Sweden and Denmark remained negligible or zero, but not simply because of a failure to meet the criteria. They will actively choose not to join, the analysts said.
In Britain, the prospect of a new Labour government after the May 1 election means that EMU will probably take a back seat, possibly for years, until a full domestic agenda is handled.
In Denmark and Sweden, constitutional obstacles have been raised to EMU and public opinion seems to be turning against federalism, the analysts said.
Only one of 38 respondents answering the question rated the chances of Italy being in EMU at the start at 100 percent, despite Rome's eagerness to join...(corrects number of responses and clarifies).

They said most of the measures to reduce the budget deficit to within the Maastricht limits were one-off and the 1997 mini-budget unveiled late last month by Prime Minister Romano Prodi was disappointing.

"Prodi is determined that Italy will be in EMU at the start, but most of the other countries, with the exception of France, are determined that the volatile Italian currency will not sabotage the single currency budget," said an economist at an Italian bank.

"Italy has not achieved credibility and the European central bank will not have credibility if the lira is included in the euro. France wants Italy in because they are worried about the effect of a devalued lira on their export industries. But they will have to choose between EMU and Italy."

The proportion of people thinking Spain and Portugal had a 100 percent chance of entry at the start was five percent and eight percent respectively compared with 18 and 24 percent last month (clarifies percentages).
Both countries are seen likely to make better headway than Italy in achieving the criteria, but politically it would be difficult for Spain and Portugal to enter while Italy is left in the cold.

"We don't believe EMU will start with a broad base. Italy won't join. If Spain and Portugal do, given the small size of their economies, the resultant volatility and instability will be limited," said Hans Honig, economist at Rabobank in Amsterdam.
